chunks: "Both extremes cause trouble, so I try to use the slowest edge that still meets timing. If the edge is too slow, the signal spends a long time near the receiver's threshold.
Any noise on the line moves the crossing time by noise divided by slew rate, so slow edges mean more jitter and, with enough noise, multiple crossings and glitches.
It also eats the setup budget because the crossing happens later.
On CMOS inputs it makes both transistors conduct while the input is mid-supply, so you get extra shoot-through current and sometimes oscillation on the output.
I've seen that on slow RC-filtered inputs without a Schmitt trigger.
If the edge is too fast, the line starts acting like a transmission line, so any impedance mismatch makes reflections and ringing.
The fast edge also couples into neighbours as crosstalk, makes large current spikes that cause ground bounce, and puts more energy at high frequency, which means EMI.
The usual fix is a series resistor, slew-rate control or termination."
